modules.title: Introduction to C++ and User Defined Functions

topics.title: Introduction to C++
topics.definition: C++ is a general purpose language that extends C with classes and objects, giving both low level control and object oriented features.

children.title: Applications of C++
children.definition: Used for operating systems, games, embedded software, banking systems, compilers and performance critical libraries.

children.title: History and features of C++
children.definition: Developed by Bjarne Stroustrup as C with classes; features include classes, objects, encapsulation, polymorphism, templates and exception handling.

children.title: C++ versus C
children.definition: C is procedural with no classes, while C++ supports objects, function overloading, references, namespaces and the standard template library.

topics.title: Structure of a Simple C++ Program
topics.definition: A C++ program has preprocessor directives, a main function and statements, with optional class and function definitions above main.

children.title: Header files and preprocessor directives
children.definition: Lines beginning with # such as #include <iostream> pull in library declarations before compilation.

children.title: Namespace std
children.definition: A container that holds library names like cout, so you must write std::cout or add using namespace std.

children.title: The main function
children.definition: The entry point returning an int status code, where execution begins and ends.

children.title: Comments and indentation
children.definition: Single line // comments and block /* */ comments keep the code readable and are ignored by the compiler.

topics.title: Compiling and Executing C++ Programs
topics.definition: The source file passes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly and linking to become an executable.

children.title: Preprocessor stage
children.definition: Expands directives such as #include and #define before the actual compilation.

children.title: Compiler and assembler stages
children.definition: The compiler turns source into object code and the assembler produces machine level object files.

children.title: Linker stage
children.definition: Joins the object files with library code to produce the final executable.

children.title: Runtime errors and debugging
children.definition: Syntax errors are caught by the compiler while logic errors surface only while running, so debugging with breakpoints is used.

topics.title: Programming Elements
topics.definition: The basic building blocks of a program are tokens, data types, variables, constants, operators and control statements.

children.title: Tokens, keywords and identifiers
children.definition: The smallest units such as keywords, identifiers, constants, strings and operators that the compiler recognises.

children.title: Data types and variables
children.definition: Fundamental types int, float, double, char and bool with modifiers, plus user defined types such as class.

children.title: Operators and expressions
children.definition: Arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, increment and bitwise operators combine operands into expressions.

children.title: Control statements
children.definition: Selection with if, if else and switch, and repetition with for, while and do while.

children.title: Input and output with cin and cout
children.definition: Stream operators >> and << read from the keyboard and write to the screen.

topics.title: C++ Library Functions
topics.definition: The standard library supplies ready made functions grouped in headers such as iostream, cmath, cstring and cstdlib.

children.title: iostream and string functions
children.definition: Provide stream input output and text manipulation such as strlen, strcpy and strcmp.

children.title: math and utility functions
children.definition: sqrt, pow, abs, ceil and floor come from cmath; rand and atoi come from cstdlib.

children.title: Why libraries are used
children.definition: Reusing tested library code shortens development time and reduces programming errors.

topics.title: User Defined Functions
topics.definition: A user defined function packages a task with a name, a parameter list and a return type so it can be called repeatedly.

children.title: Function declaration, definition and call
children.definition: The prototype announces the signature, the definition holds the body and the call passes control with arguments.

children.title: Return values and void functions
children.definition: A function returns one value of the stated type, or returns nothing when declared void.

children.title: Actual and formal parameters
children.definition: Actual parameters are the values passed at the call site; formal parameters are the names receiving them inside the function.

children.title: Default arguments and inline functions
children.definition: Default values let some arguments be omitted, and inline functions expand the body at the call site to avoid call overhead.

topics.title: Parameter Passing: Call by Value and Call by Reference
topics.definition: Call by value copies the argument so the original is unchanged, while call by reference passes the address so the function can modify the caller variable.

children.title: Call by value
children.definition: A duplicate of the value reaches the function, so changes stay local - swapping two numbers this way does not work.

children.title: Call by reference using references
children.definition: The reference parameter is another name for the same variable, so changes are visible to the caller.

children.title: Call by address using pointers
children.definition: The pointer parameter holds the address, and the function dereferences it to modify the original value.

children.title: Choosing between them
children.definition: Use call by value for small read only data and call by reference for large objects or when results must come back through parameters.

modules.title: Object Oriented Concepts, Classes, Overloading and Inheritance

topics.title: Object Oriented Programming Paradigm
topics.definition: OOP organises a program around objects that combine data and the functions that operate on that data.

children.title: Procedural versus object oriented approach
children.definition: Procedural programming follows functions and global data, while OOP follows objects with encapsulated state and behaviour.

children.title: Basic OOP concepts
children.definition: The core ideas are class, object, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism and message passing.

children.title: Benefits of OOP
children.definition: Reusability through inheritance, easier maintenance, data security by encapsulation and natural modelling of real world entities.

children.title: Applications of OOP
children.definition: Used in simulation, GUI software, databases, CAD systems and large business applications.

topics.title: C++ Class Definition and Member Functions
topics.definition: A class is a user defined type that bundles data members and member functions, and an object is one instance of that class.

children.title: Class specification and access specifiers
children.definition: Members are declared private, protected or public; private members are reachable only inside the class.

children.title: Member functions inside and outside the class
children.definition: Small functions can be defined inline in the class, while larger ones are declared inside and defined outside using the scope resolution operator.

children.title: Objects and memory
children.definition: Each object gets its own copy of the data members, while member functions are shared by all objects of the class.

children.title: The this pointer
children.definition: A hidden pointer inside every member function that refers to the object on which the function was called.

topics.title: Static Members
topics.definition: A static data member is shared by all objects of the class and a static member function can be called without any object.

children.title: Static data member
children.definition: Declared inside the class and defined once outside; only one copy exists for the whole class.

children.title: Static member function
children.definition: Has no this pointer, so it can access only static members and other static functions.

children.title: Use cases
children.definition: Counting the number of objects created, keeping shared configuration values and implementing utility functions.

topics.title: Constructors and Destructors
topics.definition: A constructor initialises an object when it is created, and a destructor releases its resources when it is destroyed.

children.title: Default constructor
children.definition: Takes no arguments and is supplied by the compiler if no constructor is written.

children.title: Parameterised constructor
children.definition: Accepts arguments so an object can be created with initial values, as in Student s(101, "Ravi").

children.title: Copy constructor
children.definition: Creates a new object as a copy of another, taking a reference to the same class; needed to avoid shallow copying of pointers.

children.title: Dynamic constructor
children.definition: Allocates memory at run time using new, which the destructor must free with delete.

children.title: Destructor
children.definition: Named with a tilde, takes no arguments and runs automatically when the object goes out of scope or is deleted.

children.title: Constructor overloading
children.definition: Several constructors with different parameter lists let objects be built in different ways.

topics.title: Operator Overloading
topics.definition: Operator overloading gives an extra meaning to an existing operator so it works on user defined types such as complex numbers.

children.title: Unary operator overloading
children.definition: Operators with one operand, such as ++, -- and unary minus, are overloaded with no argument or with a dummy int for postfix.

children.title: Binary operator overloading
children.definition: Operators with two operands such as +, - and * are overloaded with one parameter, or as friend functions with two.

children.title: Rules of operator overloading
children.definition: New operators cannot be invented, precedence and arity cannot change, and operators such as :: and sizeof cannot be overloaded.

children.title: Type conversions
children.definition: Conversion between basic and user defined types is done by constructor conversion and by conversion operator functions.

topics.title: Function Overloading, Friend and Virtual Functions
topics.definition: C++ allows several functions with the same name but different parameter lists, and provides friend and virtual functions for special access and late binding.

children.title: Function overloading
children.definition: The compiler picks the correct version from the number or types of the arguments - the return type alone cannot distinguish them.

children.title: Friend function and friend class
children.definition: A non member function or another class granted access to the private members of the class that declares it.

children.title: Virtual function
children.definition: A member function declared virtual is chosen at run time based on the actual object, which is how runtime polymorphism works.

children.title: Pure virtual function and abstract class
children.definition: A virtual function with no body makes the class abstract, so objects cannot be created but derived classes must implement it.

children.title: Static versus dynamic binding
children.definition: Normal calls are resolved at compile time while virtual calls are resolved at run time through the vtable.

topics.title: Inheritance and Its Types
topics.definition: Inheritance lets a new class reuse and extend the members of an existing class, expressing an is-a relationship.

children.title: Base and derived class
children.definition: The base class supplies common members and the derived class adds or overrides behaviour.

children.title: Single inheritance
children.definition: One derived class inherits from exactly one base class.

children.title: Multiple inheritance
children.definition: One derived class inherits from more than one base class, which can cause ambiguity between same named members.

children.title: Multilevel inheritance
children.definition: A chain such as A to B to C, where each level inherits from the previous one.

children.title: Hierarchical inheritance
children.definition: Several classes inherit from one common base class.

children.title: Hybrid inheritance
children.definition: A combination of two or more inheritance forms, usually built from multiple and multilevel.

children.title: Virtual base class
children.definition: Declaring a base virtual ensures that only one copy of its members survives the diamond problem of multiple inheritance.

children.title: Applications of inheritance
children.definition: Code reuse, building class libraries and frameworks, and modelling taxonomies such as Shape and Circle.

modules.title: Java Applets, Graphics, Files and Collections

topics.title: Introduction to Java Applet Programming
topics.definition: An applet is a small Java program that used to be embedded in a web page and executed inside the browser.

children.title: What an applet is
children.definition: A class extending Applet or JApplet whose execution is controlled by the browser or applet viewer.

children.title: Applet life cycle
children.definition: init, start, paint, stop and destroy are called by the browser at the appropriate moments.

children.title: Applet versus application
children.definition: An application starts at main and runs on its own, while an applet has no main, is embedded in HTML and is restricted by the browser sandbox.

children.title: Why applets are obsolete
children.definition: Browsers removed plugin support, so applets are replaced by Java Web Start and modern web technologies.

topics.title: Graphic Programming in Java
topics.definition: The Graphics class provides drawing primitives for lines, rectangles, ovals, polygons, strings and images.

children.title: Coordinate system and Graphics object
children.definition: The origin is the top left corner and the Graphics object supplied to paint performs all drawing.

children.title: Drawing shapes and text
children.definition: Methods such as drawLine, drawRect, fillRect, drawOval, drawPolygon and drawString draw the primitives.

children.title: Colours and fonts
children.definition: setColor with the Color class and setFont with the Font class control appearance.

children.title: Animation basics
children.definition: Shapes are redrawn in a loop after a delay, usually inside the paint method, to create movement.

topics.title: Managing Input and Output Files
topics.definition: Java file handling reads and writes data through stream classes, with character streams for text and byte streams for binary data.

children.title: File and FileWriter or FileReader
children.definition: The File class represents a path while FileReader and FileWriter transfer characters to and from a file.

children.title: BufferedReader and BufferedWriter
children.definition: Wrap the character streams to buffer data, which reduces the number of slow disk operations.

children.title: Streams versus readers
children.definition: InputStream and OutputStream work on bytes while Reader and Writer work on characters with encoding.

children.title: Exception handling during file operations
children.definition: File operations throw IOException, so try, catch and finally blocks are required.

topics.title: Java Collections Framework
topics.definition: The collections framework provides ready made data structures such as lists, sets, maps and queues together with iterators.

children.title: Lists: ArrayList and LinkedList
children.definition: ArrayList keeps a growable array with fast index access; LinkedList uses nodes and is faster for insertion at the ends.

children.title: Sets: HashSet and TreeSet
children.definition: HashSet stores unique elements without order while TreeSet keeps them sorted.

children.title: Maps: HashMap and TreeMap
children.definition: Store key value pairs; HashMap has no order while TreeMap iterates in sorted key order.

children.title: Queue and Deque interfaces
children.definition: Used for FIFO and double ended queue behaviour, with PriorityQueue for priority order.

children.title: Iterator and the for-each loop
children.definition: The Iterator walks through a collection and may remove elements safely during traversal.

children.title: Comparison with arrays
children.definition: Collections resize automatically, hold objects and provide algorithms such as sort and search through the Collections class.

topics.title: Event Handling
topics.definition: Event handling responds to user actions by notifying listener objects that the event has occurred.

children.title: Delegation event model
children.definition: A source generates an event object and sends it to registered listener objects that implement the matching interface.

children.title: Event classes
children.definition: ActionEvent, MouseEvent, KeyEvent, ItemEvent and WindowEvent carry details such as source and modifiers.

children.title: Listener interfaces and adapter classes
children.definition: ActionListener, MouseListener and KeyListener receive events, and adapter classes provide empty implementations of their methods.

children.title: Registering listeners
children.definition: addActionListener, addMouseListener and addKeyListener connect a component to its handler.

children.title: Common statements inside a handler
children.definition: Determining the source and performing the required action such as validating a form or closing a window.

topics.title: AWT: Working with Windows, Graphics and Text
topics.definition: The Abstract Window Toolkit provides the original Java classes for windows, controls, graphics and text.

children.title: Frame and window basics
children.definition: Frame creates a top level window with a title bar, while Panel groups components inside it.

children.title: Components and containers
children.definition: Controls are added to containers such as Frame and Panel using add.

children.title: Drawing on a component
children.definition: The paint method draws lines, shapes and text on the component surface.

children.title: Text output with fonts
children.definition: drawString plus the Font and FontMetrics classes position and measure text.

topics.title: AWT Controls
topics.definition: AWT supplies standard controls for user input, each with its own event type.

children.title: Labels and buttons
children.definition: Label displays fixed text and Button raises an ActionEvent when clicked.

children.title: Text fields and text areas
children.definition: TextField accepts one line and TextArea accepts multiple lines of input.

children.title: Checkbox, choice and list
children.definition: Checkbox toggles a state, Choice is a drop down list and List shows a scrollable list of items.

children.title: Scrollbars and layout within controls
children.definition: Scrollbar values generate adjustment events and are used for sliders or scrolling.

topics.title: Layout Managers and Menus
topics.definition: Layout managers decide the position and size of components, and menus provide a standard menu bar interface.

children.title: FlowLayout
children.definition: Arranges components left to right and wraps to the next line, like words on a page.

children.title: BorderLayout
children.definition: Places components in five regions: north, south, east, west and centre.

children.title: GridLayout and CardLayout
children.definition: GridLayout arranges components in equal sized cells, CardLayout stacks components so only one is visible at a time.

children.title: GridBagLayout
children.definition: The most flexible manager, using constraints for grid position, weight and fill of each component.

children.title: MenuBar, Menu and MenuItem
children.definition: A frame holds one menu bar, each menu holds items, and selecting an item raises an action event.

topics.title: Working with Images
topics.definition: Images are loaded with getImage or ImageIcon and drawn with drawImage, and can be manipulated pixel by pixel.

children.title: Loading an image
children.definition: getImage needs an applet or Toolkit context, while ImageIcon works in any application.

children.title: Drawing an image
children.definition: drawImage paints it at a position and with an optional size, and it may load asynchronously.

children.title: Image processing basics
children.definition: Pixel arrays from PixelGrabber allow filters, cropping and resizing.

modules.title: Java Swing, Java Beans and Servlets

topics.title: Java Swing and Its Controls
topics.definition: Swing is a lightweight component library built on AWT that provides richer and platform independent controls.

children.title: JFrame, JPanel and container hierarchy
children.definition: JFrame is the top level window, its content pane holds components and JPanel groups them.

children.title: Common Swing controls
children.definition: JButton, JLabel, JTextField, JTextArea, JCheckBox, JRadioButton, JComboBox, JList and JTable.

children.title: Swing versus AWT
children.definition: Swing components are lightweight and drawn by Java, AWT components are heavyweight and depend on the operating system.

children.title: Dialogs and message boxes
children.definition: JOptionPane shows messages and collects simple input without building a whole form.

children.title: Menus and toolbars in Swing
children.definition: JMenuBar, JMenu and JMenuItem together with JToolBar create the standard application interface.

topics.title: Java Beans
topics.definition: A Java Bean is a reusable software component that follows naming conventions so tools can inspect and manipulate it.

children.title: Properties of a bean
children.definition: Private fields exposed through getter and setter methods that follow the getX and setX pattern.

children.title: Introspection
children.definition: Tools discover a bean properties, methods and events automatically from the naming conventions.

children.title: Events and bound properties
children.definition: A bean can notify listeners when a property changes using the event model.

children.title: Bean Development Kit usage
children.definition: The BDK allowed beans to be assembled visually in a builder tool without writing code.

children.title: Advantages of beans
children.definition: Reusability, visual assembly and configuration through properties.

topics.title: Servlets
topics.definition: A servlet is a Java class that runs on a web server and generates dynamic web content in response to HTTP requests.

children.title: Servlet life cycle
children.definition: The container calls init once, service for every request and destroy before removing it.

children.title: HttpServlet and doGet or doPost
children.definition: GET carries parameters in the URL for retrieval, POST carries them in the request body for submission.

children.title: Request and response objects
children.definition: HttpServletRequest supplies parameters and HttpServletResponse writes the reply, with content type set first.

children.title: Session tracking
children.definition: Cookies, hidden form fields and HttpSession maintain state between separate HTTP requests.

children.title: Servlet versus CGI
children.definition: Servlets stay loaded in memory and handle each request in a thread, while CGI starts a new process per request.

children.title: Deployment
children.definition: A web.xml descriptor or annotations map URLs to servlet classes inside a web container such as Tomcat.
